scenario: Your API calls a recommendation service with no timeout. When that service hangs, all of your API's worker threads end up stuck waiting and the whole site stops responding.
prompt: What is the first thing to add?

options.text: More API worker threads
A bigger server for the recommendation service
Logging on every call
A timeout on the call, with a fallback when it fires

explanation: Without a timeout, one slow dependency holds every thread hostage. A short timeout plus a fallback (for example, no recommendations) keeps the core site up. More threads just take longer to all get stuck.

scenario: Each user may make 5 requests per second on average, but short bursts of up to 20 requests should be allowed.

options.text: Token bucket: refill 5 tokens/s, bucket size 20
Fixed window: at most 5 requests per calendar second
Block the user after 20 total requests
An unbounded queue for every user

explanation: A token bucket enforces the average rate through its refill speed and allows bursts up to the bucket size. A 5-per-second fixed window would reject any burst.

scenario: During a network partition between two data centers, the shopping cart service keeps accepting writes in both.
prompt: What did it give up, and what must it handle later?

options.text: Availability; it must replay the rejected writes
Strong consistency; it must merge conflicting carts when the partition heals
Partition tolerance; nothing needs handling
Durability; it must restore from backups

explanation: Staying available on both sides of a partition means the two copies can diverge (an AP choice under CAP). When the link returns, the carts must be reconciled, for example by merging their items.

prompt: Why run at least two instances of a service in different availability zones?

options.text: If one zone goes down, the other keeps serving traffic
It is cheaper than one instance
Deploys finish faster
Logs get smaller

explanation: Availability zones fail independently (power, network). Spreading instances across them removes a single point of failure.

scenario: A downstream service is failing. Your code keeps calling it on every request, each call waits for a timeout, and your own latency balloons.

options.text: Retry each failed call five times immediately
Increase the timeout
A circuit breaker that fails fast for a while, then tests whether the service recovered
Cache the error responses forever

explanation: After enough failures the breaker opens and calls fail instantly instead of waiting. After a cool-down it lets a few test calls through and closes again once they succeed.

scenario: Last month the whole site was down for 40 minutes when a single virtual machine rebooted.
prompt: Tap the single point of failure.

options.text: Users
Load balancer x2
API x6
Auth service
User DB

explanation: Everything else is redundant, but every request needs the auth service and it runs on one instance with no failover. When its VM rebooted, nothing could authenticate.

prompt: Put the steps of handling a production incident in order.

options.text: An alert fires on the rising error rate
Mitigate: roll back or fail over to restore service
Investigate and confirm the root cause
Write a blameless postmortem with action items

explanation: Restore service first, then dig into the root cause once users are no longer affected, then capture lessons so it does not recur.

scenario: The recommendation service is down. The product page normally shows a 'You might also like' row from it.
prompt: What should the product page do?

options.text: Return a 500 error
Retry until the recommendation service answers
Redirect to an error page
Show the page without that row, or with a cached default list

explanation: Graceful degradation: a non-essential feature failing should not take down the core experience. Customers can still view and buy the product.

scenario: After you post, you see your own post immediately, but your friends only see it a few seconds later.
prompt: Which consistency model describes this system?

options.text: Eventual consistency with read-your-writes
Strong (linearizable) consistency
No consistency guarantees at all
Two-phase commit

explanation: Everyone converges on the same data after a delay (eventual), and the author is guaranteed to see their own write right away (read-your-writes). Strong consistency would show friends the post immediately too.

scenario: Each API instance's health check endpoint runs a database query. During a 20-second database blip, the load balancer marks every API instance unhealthy and removes all of them.

options.text: Health-check every 1 second instead of every 10
Keep the load balancer check shallow (is this process alive?), and alert on dependency health separately
Remove health checks
Add more API instances

explanation: A shared dependency in the health check makes every instance fail at once, turning a brief database blip into a total outage. The load balancer should only remove instances that are themselves broken.
